opus-5.5.text:
What strikes me most about Marc is his persistence. He has worked on essentially one problem for more than forty years: how to make machines move with the dynamic balance that animals have. Back in the early eighties, in his Leg Lab at Carnegie Mellon and then MIT, he was building one-legged hopping robots. Most people saw them as strange toys. Walking robots back then were slow and statically stable, always keeping their center of mass over their feet. Marc's insight was the opposite: let the robot be unstable, let it fall, and control the falling. That's how animals move, and it's why Boston Dynamics machines look so alive.

The second thing is his taste. He cares a lot about how a robot looks when it moves, almost like an artist. The videos, like the dog being kicked and recovering, or the robots dancing, aren't just marketing. He believes motion itself communicates whether you've really solved the problem. If it looks wrong, it probably is wrong.

Third, he's comfortable working outside the usual timelines. The company changed hands several times, through Google, SoftBank, and Hyundai, and for years people asked where the products and revenue were. He kept protecting the long-term research culture, and that bet is a big part of why humanoids and legged robots feel so real today.

And finally, he's playful. He'll talk about robots doing parkour or dancing with real joy. I think that curiosity, more than any business plan, is what has kept him going.

fable-5.1.text:
What strikes me most about Marc Raibert is how long his horizon is. He started working on legged locomotion in the late seventies at Carnegie Mellon, then the MIT Leg Lab, with those one-legged hopping machines, and he was still chasing the same question forty years later: how do you make a machine move the way an animal moves? Most founders pivot when the market doesn't show up. He just kept going.

The second thing is that he's a scientist first, not a businessman. Boston Dynamics spent most of its life as a research shop funded by DARPA, and Marc never pretended otherwise. When Google bought them, then SoftBank, then Hyundai, he basically treated each owner as a new patron who'd fund the next decade of experiments. He wasn't optimizing for an exit. He was optimizing for the robot getting better.

Third, he had taste. You can see it in the videos. BigDog getting kicked and recovering, Atlas doing parkour. Those weren't marketing stunts in the beginning; they were honest demonstrations of dynamic balance, and the honesty is why they went viral. He built an engineering culture where the demo had to actually work, and where "it fell over" was interesting data rather than a failure to hide.

And the last piece is his skepticism about hype. He's always been very frank that the humanoid form is hard, that full autonomy is far away, that a lot of what people see in a clip takes months of tuning. In an industry full of people selling the future, he kept insisting on the physics. I think that's why, even now, when every company is showing a humanoid, people still look to Boston Dynamics as the benchmark for what real capability looks like.
